alignment.note: Greek demonstrative ἐκεῖνοί and Latin hi correspond to Syriac ܗܠܝܢ; the Peshitta places the demonstrative after the relative clause, reflecting a different word order, but the semantic equivalence is intact.

The Greek substantival article οἱ (with the participle σπαρέντες) and the Latin relative qui head the clause 'those sown'; Syriac instead fronts the locative phrase and uses a finite verb ܐܙܕܪܥܘ, so no discrete article-token corresponds, a recurring Syriac construction difference.

Greek ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν τὴν καλήν and Latin super terram bonam render the prepositional phrase analytically; Syriac compresses preposition, noun and adjective into ܕܒܐܪܥܐ ܛܒܬܐ, where the proclitic ܒ carries the locative force.

Greek uses the aorist passive participle σπαρέντες and Latin the perfect passive periphrasis seminati sunt; Syriac employs a finite ethpaʿal verb ܐܙܕܪܥܘ ('were sown'), shifting the participial construction to a main verb but preserving the passive sense.
The Greek relative οἵτινες, Latin qui, and the Syriac proclitic relative ܕ- on ܕܫܡܥܝܢ all introduce the clause describing those who hear; the relative force is folded into the verb form in Syriac.
Greek τὸν λόγον and Latin verbum render 'the word' articularly/anarthrously; Syriac ܡܠܬܐ uses the emphatic state, functionally definite, with no separate article token.
Greek παραδέχονται ('receive [it]') and Latin suscipiunt are matched by the Syriac participle ܘܡܩܒܠܝܢ, whose proclitic ܘ supplies the connective rendered separately as καί/et in the other traditions.

Greek καρποφοροῦσιν and Latin fructificant use a single denominal verb 'bear fruit'; Syriac renders idiomatically with the verb ܝܗܒ ('give') plus the object ܦܐܪܐ ('fruit'), i.e. 'give fruit', a periphrastic equivalent.

Greek ἓν and Latin unum supply the distributive 'one [yielding]' before each numeral; the Peshitta omits this distributive entirely, attaching the proclitic ܒ ('at/by') directly to each number, a typical Syriac simplification.
As before, the distributive ἓν / unum precedes 'sixty' in Greek and Latin; Syriac lacks any corresponding token, folding the sense into the prefixed numeral ܘܒܫܬܝܢ.
Greek καί and Latin et coordinate the final clause; the Syriac connective is carried by the proclitic ܘ on ܘܒܡܐܐ rather than a freestanding conjunction.
The third distributive ἓν / unum is again present in Greek and Latin but absent in Syriac, consistent with the Peshitta's economical numerical syntax throughout the verse.
Greek ἑκατόν, Latin centum and Syriac ܘܒܡܐܐ all denote 'a hundred[fold]'; the Greek paragraph mark (¶) appended to the final token is editorial and has no counterpart in the other witnesses.
